function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your own CI pipeline).  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents you’ll need to drop into the repo so that everything builds, tests, and deploys automatically.

> ⚠️ **Important** – I don’t have direct access to your machine or to GitHub, so I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git push`, or invoke the helper functions.  
> Instead, I’m showing you the *exact* commands and file templates you should use. Once you run them locally (or in your own CI job) they will create the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow, stage them, commit, and push to the remote.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’re cloning over HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo (optional)

If you want to confirm the dominant language before generating the Dockerfile, you can run the helper function (or simply eyeball the repo).  
Assuming the repo contains a standard Node.js project (`package.json` + `src/`), the dominant language will be **JavaScript** (or TypeScript).

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build the application (if you have a build script)
RUN npm run build || true

# Final stage
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only built artifacts from the builder stage
COPY --from=builder /app .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses a lightweight Alpine image.  
> * Builds in a separate stage so that only production dependencies are shipped.  
> * Falls back gracefully if there’s no `build` script.  
> * Exposes port **3000**, which is the default for many Express apps.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- adjust if you use a different registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # External port exposed by the service
    targetPort: 3000          # Port inside the pod
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas of the container.  
> * Exposes the app through a LoadBalancer (cloud provider will allocate an IP).  
> * Maps external port 80 → internal port 3000.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ hashFiles('**/Dockerfile') }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://${{ vars.PROD_URL }}   # optional: set a variable in repo settings

    steps:
    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v3
      with:
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64‑encoded kubeconfig
        context: my-cluster

    - name: Deploy to cluster
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Logs into Docker Hub (you’ll need to store `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repo secrets).  
> * Builds the image and pushes it to Docker Hub.  
> * Applies the Kubernetes manifest to your cluster (store your kubeconfig as a secret called `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA`).  

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a cloud provider that supports automatic image pulls (e.g., EKS, GKE, AKS), you may skip the `deploy` job entirely and let the cluster pull the image directly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you created the `k8s/` folder manually, make sure it’s tracked too.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions CI/CD"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will kick off automatically, build the image, push it to Docker Hub, and deploy it to your Kubernetes cluster.

---

### 🎉 What you now have

| Artifact | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Containerizes the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates build, push, and deploy on every push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, service type, or image registry to fit your environment. Happy coding!
